Chapter 14 · The great schools · 1897–1960

Behaviourism and learning

Pavlov, Thorndike, Watson and Skinner: psychology as the science of observable behaviour and the laws of learning.

In the early twentieth century a group of psychologists grew tired of the endless arguments about introspection. They proposed studying only what can be observed and measured: behaviour and the conditions under which it occurs. Behaviourism dominated academic psychology in the United States for almost half a century and left laws of learning that are still used.

What were people trying to understand?

How animals and people learn, how habits and fears are acquired and lost, and whether all behaviour can be explained by the relation between stimuli, responses and consequences.

With what methods?

Controlled experiments, often with animals, in which stimuli were manipulated and behaviour recorded. The Russian physiologist Ivan Pavlov, who won the Nobel Prize in 1904 for his studies of digestion, noticed that his dogs salivated before receiving food, on seeing the assistant or hearing a sound that announced it. That is how he described classical conditioning. In the United States, Edward Thorndike shut cats in "puzzle boxes" they could escape by working a mechanism; over the trials they got out faster and faster. In 1898 he formulated the law of effect: responses that have satisfying consequences tend to be repeated.

Who took part?

John B. Watson published in 1913 an article regarded as the behaviourist manifesto: psychology should be a natural science of behaviour, without reference to consciousness. In 1920, with his assistant Rosalie Rayner, he conditioned an eleven-month-old baby, "Little Albert", to fear a white rat by pairing it with a loud noise. In 1924 Mary Cover Jones, who has been called the mother of behaviour therapy, did the reverse: she removed a child's fear of rabbits by bringing the animal closer little by little while he ate.

Clark Hull tried to express learning in equations. Edward Tolman showed that rats exploring a maze without reward learned its layout and used it once food appeared; he spoke of cognitive maps, a decidedly un-behaviourist idea. From 1938 B. F. Skinner studied operant conditioning: how reinforcers and their schedules shape behaviour. He invented the box that bears his name and applied his principles to teaching and to society.

What did it contribute?

  • Rigorous experimental methods and the requirement to define variables precisely.
  • Laws of learning used in education, parenting, health and animal training.
  • Behaviour therapy: exposure, systematic desensitisation and applied behaviour analysis.
  • Concepts such as reinforcement, extinction and generalisation, found throughout psychology today.

What was revised later?

The Little Albert experiment would be unacceptable today: the mother was not properly informed and the fear that was created was never removed. The child's identity is still debated. Watson's claim that he could turn any baby into a doctor or a thief with the right training ignored heredity, and animal studies showed that some things are learned far more easily than others, such as aversion to a taste after a single bout of sickness (Garcia, 1966). From the 1950s the cognitive revolution brought mental processes back into psychology, but many behavioural techniques remain among the best validated.

"Give me a dozen healthy infants [...] and I'll guarantee to take any one at random and train him to become any type of specialist I might select" (Watson, 1924). The passage goes on: "I am going beyond my facts and I admit it."

  1. Pavlov, I. P. (1927). Conditioned Reflexes (trad. G. V. Anrep). Londres: Oxford University Press.
  2. Thorndike, E. L. (1898). Animal intelligence. Psychological Review Monograph Supplements, 2(4).
  3. Watson, J. B. (1913). Psychology as the behaviorist views it. Psychological Review, 20(2), 158–177.
  4. Watson, J. B. y Rayner, R. (1920). Conditioned emotional reactions. Journal of Experimental Psychology, 3(1), 1–14.
  5. Jones, M. C. (1924). A laboratory study of fear: The case of Peter. Pedagogical Seminary, 31(4), 308–315.
